title: Trends in research related to "Shinrin-yoku” (taking in the forest atmosphere or forest bathing) in Japan
review_question: What are the trends and physiological effects of 'Shinrin-yoku' (forest bathing) research in Japan, focusing on sensory elements and field studies?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly stated, but focuses on studies conducted in Japan related to Shinrin-yoku, including laboratory and field experiments, with a particular emphasis on physiological measurements and sensory elements.

synthesis_conclusions: Continued accumulation of scientific evidence is needed to firmly anchor 'Shinrin-yoku' in society and fully exploit its therapeutic effects.
There is a need to increase the variety of forest settings appropriate for 'Shinrin-yoku' and to develop novel systems for evaluating its effects.

Research on individual differences (age, physical strength, personal preference, physiological character, personality) is required to enable experts to devise individually tailored 'Shinrin-yoku' programs.
Salivary biomarkers (cortisol, IgA, amylase activity, chromogranin A) are potential simple indices for on-the-spot assessment of 'Shinrin-yoku' effects.
The effects of forest environments on human health are expected to be verified through international efforts.
evidence_gaps: Further research on the effects of individual differences (age, physical strength, personal preference, physiological character, and personality) is needed to devise individually tailored 'Shinrin-yoku' programs.
Fundamental analysis of diurnal variation and individual differences in baseline concentrations is needed to enhance the reliability of salivary amylase activity as a stress index.
Further studies on individual differences (age, dental experiences, etc.) are required to implement the idea of masking alarming sounds with gentle stream sounds into practice.

moderators.effect: Chronically stressed individuals experienced greater beneficial effects from Shinrin-yoku.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Individuals with higher self-rated psychological stress levels experienced greater beneficial effects.

moderators.effect: Weak concentrations induced relaxation, while strong concentrations induced stress.
moderators.subgroup_effects: 10 µL/30 L and 100 µL/30 L concentrations decreased systolic blood pressure; 500 µL/30 L concentration increased pulse rate and prefrontal activity.

moderators.effect: An appropriate wood quantity (30% ratio) induced physiological relaxation, while excessive amounts (90% ratio) caused an awakened response after initial relaxation.
moderators.subgroup_effects: 30% wood ratio decreased pulse rate and diastolic blood pressure; 90% wood ratio initially decreased blood pressure but subsequently increased pulse rate and prefrontal activity.

moderators.effect: Nature-video clips were effective in normalizing stress-induced cardiovascular responses in Type A individuals.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Nature-video clips normalized stress-induced cardiovascular responses in Type A individuals, showing no significant differences between Type A and B subjects in recovery.

limitations: Field studies face challenges in controlling experimental conditions such as weather and temperature, requiring large sample sizes to improve signal-to-noise ratio.
Prior to the 'Therapeutic Effects of Forests' project, established methods for physiological measurements in the field were lacking, leading to a predominance of laboratory-based studies.

Laboratory experiments on olfactory compounds may involve relatively high concentrations, making it difficult to rule out direct blood-borne effects in addition to olfactory pathway effects, unlike lower atmospheric concentrations in field settings.
Ambiguous results in some early studies (e.g., Ohira et al. [40] for EEG/ECG) were attributed to low temperatures in the forest due to bad weather.
